items.q: When I (A) have arrived at the stadium last night, the match (B) had already started and the crowd (C) was cheering (D) loudly.
items.explanation: A finished action with a past time expression (last night) takes the past simple, never the present perfect: arrived.

items.q: Each of the paintings in the new gallery (A) on the second floor (B) were created by artists (C) who grew up (D) in this small coastal town.
items.explanation: The subject is each, which is singular; the plural noun paintings sits inside a prepositional phrase and does not control the verb.

items.q: After (A) a long day of hiking, we (B) finally reached (C) top of the mountain and (D) watched the sun set over the valley.
items.explanation: A singular countable noun cannot stand alone; top of a specific mountain is unique, so it needs the definite article: the top.

items.q: The tourists (A) who booked the early train (B) were disappointed when it (C) finally arrived (D) to the station nearly an hour late.
items.explanation: Arrive is never followed by to: we arrive at a building or small place and in a city or country.

items.q: The (A) succeed of the school football team this season (B) is largely due to (C) the new coach, who (D) trains them twice a week.
items.explanation: After the and before of we need a noun, not a verb: success (noun), succeed (verb), successful (adjective).

items.q: Students (A) who forget (B) his homework will have to (C) stay after class and (D) finish it under the teacher's supervision.
options: finish it under the teacher's supervision
items.explanation: The possessive must agree with its noun: students is plural, so the homework is their homework, not his.

items.q: The winter (A) in the north of the country (B) is usually (C) much more colder than (D) in the south, where snow almost never falls.
options: in the north of the country
items.explanation: A one-syllable adjective forms its comparative with -er alone; adding more as well makes a double comparative, which is wrong.

items.q: If the farmers (A) had known about the flood earlier, they (B) would have moved their animals (C) to higher ground and (D) will have saved most of the crops.
items.explanation: This is a third conditional about an unreal past; both verbs in the result clause need would have + past participle, so will is impossible here.

items.q: The guide (A) told to us that the ancient temple (B) had been built (C) more than a thousand years earlier by (D) local craftsmen.
options: more than a thousand years earlier
items.explanation: In reported speech tell takes a direct object with no preposition: told us that; it is say to us that needs to.

items.q: The small village (A) in the mountains (B) where we visited last summer (C) has no electricity, (D) yet the people there seem very happy.
items.explanation: Visit is a transitive verb and needs an object, so the relative pronoun must be which/that; where is only used when the clause is already complete without an object.

items.q: The teacher asked (A) the new student (B) politely (C) where was he from and (D) whether he had studied English before.
options: whether he had studied English before
items.explanation: In an indirect question the subject comes before the verb and there is no inversion: where he was from, exactly like the second part whether he had studied.

items.q: Before the storm hit, the fishermen (A) had tied their boats (B) tightly to the pier and (C) gone home to (D) do some rest.
items.explanation: The natural collocation is get (or have) some rest; do some rest is not an English expression.

items.q: There (A) were too much people at the concert last night, (B) so we (C) could hardly see the stage (D) from where we stood.
items.explanation: People is a plural countable noun, so it takes many; much is used only with uncountable nouns such as noise or time.

items.q: (A) Although the recipe looked simple, (B) but my sister (C) spent nearly three hours (D) preparing the dish for our grandmother's birthday.
items.explanation: Although already joins the two clauses, so but must be dropped; when the first clause starts with although, the main clause cannot start with but.

items.q: My father (A) has been a fan of this football club (B) since he (C) is a boy, and he (D) still watches every match on television.
options: has been a fan of this football club
items.explanation: After since the clause gives the starting point in the past, so it takes the past simple: since he was a boy.

items.q: Neither the coach (A) nor the players (B) were happy (C) with the result, (D) which were announced after the final whistle.
items.explanation: The relative pronoun which refers to the result (singular), so its verb must be singular; were happy is correct because with neither … nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the players.

items.q: Every morning (A) sun rises behind the hills (B) at about six, and (C) the farmers are already (D) at work in the rice fields by then.
options: at work in the rice fields
items.correction: the sun rises behind the hills
items.explanation: Things that are unique in our world take the: the sun, the moon, the sky; the noun cannot appear with no article at all.

items.q: My aunt (A) has been interested (B) on photography (C) since she received (D) her first camera as a birthday present.
items.explanation: The adjective interested is always followed by in; keen on takes on, but interested on does not exist.

items.q: Doctors (A) constantly remind us that regular exercise (B) can improve not only (C) our physically health but also (D) our mood and sleep.
items.explanation: A noun (health) is described by an adjective, physical; the adverb physically can only modify a verb or an adjective.

items.q: The old man (A) who lives next door (B) keeps a garden (C) so beautiful that (D) it's flowers attract visitors from other streets.
items.explanation: The possessive of it is its with no apostrophe; it's is always the short form of it is or it has.

items.q: This is (A) the more interesting museum I (B) have ever visited, (C) partly because visitors (D) are allowed to touch many of the exhibits.
items.explanation: The pattern the + superlative + I have ever … compares one thing with all others, so it needs the superlative most, not the comparative more.

items.q: If you (A) mix yellow and blue paint, you (B) would get green, (C) which is why (D) art teachers always start with the primary colours.
items.explanation: Mixing yellow and blue is a fact that is always true, so this is a zero (or first) conditional: if you mix …, you get / will get green; would belongs to the unreal second conditional.

items.q: When I got home, my mother (A) immediately asked me (B) in a worried voice (C) that I had finished my homework (D) before going out to play.
options: that I had finished my homework
items.correction: whether I had finished my homework
items.explanation: A reported yes/no question is introduced by whether or if; that is only used to report statements.

items.q: The astronaut (A) who spoke to our class (B) described the feeling of (C) looking down at Earth, (D) what she said was unforgettable.
items.explanation: A relative clause adding a comment about a noun (the feeling) is introduced by which; what means the thing that and cannot follow a noun in this way.

items.q: My cousin (A) speaks very well English because she (B) spent two years (C) studying in Australia (D) while her parents worked there.
items.explanation: An adverb of manner does not come between a verb and its object; the order is verb + object + adverb: speaks English very well.

items.q: Our science teacher (A) encouraged us to (B) make an experiment (C) at home (D) using only salt, water and a candle.
options: using only salt, water and a candle
items.explanation: The verb that collocates with experiment is do (or carry out); make an experiment is a common learner error.

items.q: We (A) have only five minutes left, (B) so (C) every students should (D) stop writing and hand in their papers now.
options: stop writing and hand in their papers now
items.explanation: Every is always followed by a singular countable noun: every student; for a plural noun use all students.

items.q: The museum (A) was closed for repairs, (B) so we (C) spent the afternoon walking in the park (D) despite it was raining.
options: spent the afternoon walking in the park
items.explanation: Despite is a preposition and must be followed by a noun or -ing form (despite the rain); a full clause with a subject and verb needs the conjunction although.

items.q: (A) One of my classmates have won a scholarship to study abroad, (B) which (C) surprised nobody because (D) she works harder than anyone.
options: One of my classmates have won
items.correction: One of my classmates has won
items.explanation: The head of the subject is one, which is singular; classmates only belongs to the of phrase, so the verb must be has won.

items.q: By the time we (A) reached the beach, the tide (B) has gone out and (C) the children (D) were collecting shells on the wet sand.
items.explanation: By the time + past simple signals that the other action was completed earlier in the past, which requires the past perfect: had gone out.

items.q: The old photographs (A) hanging on the wall (B) remind my grandfather (C) about his childhood (D) in a small fishing village.
items.explanation: When something makes you think of the past, the pattern is remind somebody of something; remind somebody about is only used for a duty or appointment.

items.q: My sister (A) wants to become (B) an engineer, (C) so she (D) spends most of her free time studying the maths.
options: spends most of her free time studying the maths
items.correction: spends most of her free time studying maths
items.explanation: School subjects and fields of study used in a general sense take no article: studying maths, learning history.

items.q: The manager (A) told my sister and I that the shop (B) would close early (C) on the last day of the year (D) because of the holiday.
options: on the last day of the year
items.explanation: The pronoun is the object of told, so it must be the object form me; test it by removing the other person: told me, not told I.

items.q: The old town (A) is well known (B) for its beauty gardens, (C) which were planted (D) more than two centuries ago by a French botanist.
items.explanation: A noun (gardens) is described by the adjective beautiful; beauty is a noun and cannot do that job here.

items.q: The plants on the balcony (A) will die within a week (B) unless you (C) don't remember to water them (D) while we are away.
items.explanation: Unless already means if … not, so the verb after it is positive; a second negative reverses the meaning.

items.q: The new stadium (A) can hold nearly twice (B) as many spectators (C) as the old one, (D) but the tickets are much expensive.
options: but the tickets are much expensive
items.correction: but the tickets are much more expensive
items.explanation: Much can only strengthen a comparative, so the adjective must be in comparative form: much more expensive; much expensive is not possible.

items.q: Our neighbours (A) made a great party last weekend (B) to celebrate (C) their daughter's graduation (D) from medical school.
items.explanation: English says have, hold or throw a party; make a party is a direct translation that native speakers do not use.

items.q: The pilot announced (A) that the plane (B) will land in Hanoi in twenty minutes and (C) asked passengers (D) to fasten their seat belts.
items.explanation: The reporting verbs (announced, asked) are in the past, so the pilot's original will land is backshifted to would land, matching the past tense of the rest of the sentence.

items.q: Although the film (A) lasted almost three hours, (B) my little brother (C) enjoyed to watch every minute (D) and asked to see it again.
options: and asked to see it again
items.explanation: Enjoy belongs to the group of verbs (with mind, finish, avoid) that take an -ing form, never a to-infinitive.

items.q: We (A) wanted to hold the party at home, (B) but our living room (C) simply wasn't (D) enough big for thirty guests.
options: wanted to hold the party at home
items.explanation: Enough goes after an adjective or adverb (big enough, fast enough) but before a noun (enough space).
